newsitem.title: UK: BOE report may signal more relaxed UK rate stance.
newsitem.headline: BOE report may signal more relaxed UK rate stance.

text.p: The Bank of England's quarterly inflation report due on Tuesday is likely to suggest there is room to wait and see before increasing Britain's 6.25 percent interest rates again after last week's 1/4 point rise.
"With the mini-budget coming up, the Bank will want to wait before making any further move on monetary policy," Morgan Stanley UK economist Mark Miller said.
"The Bank is likely to take a softer stance than in the February report," he said.
In February, the Bank warned that British inflation was likely to hit 3.0 percent over the next two years without "a moderate tightening of policy".

Since then rates have increased by a modest 25 basis points but more importantly, the Bank of England was given complete control of monetary policy last week by new British Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown.
It is this new degree of independence which is likely to usher in a more relaxed attitude to interest rates.

"Logically they ought to be concluding tomorrow that rates should go up one more time but it's one thing to advise the Chancellor, it's another thing to pull the trigger yourself," NatWest Markets UK economist Geoff Dicks said.
Talking to reporters in Basle this morning, Bank of England Governor Eddie George seemed much less concerned about the state of British inflationary pressures.
"Our job is to achieve the target of inflation that the government has set of 2-1/2 percent or less. There is a better or even chance of 2-1/2 percent or less," he said.

The targeted measure of UK inflation -- retail prices excluding mortgage interest payments -- was running at an annual rate of 2.7 percent in March and data due Thursday are expected to show it declined to 2.6 percent in April.
George cited the recent strong appreciation of sterling as a one of the factors which had improved the inflation outlook.
"George is not going to be quite as hawkish as one might have assumed," commented HSBC UK economist Dharshini David.
"All his recent comments seem to suggest he thinks that interest rates are at the correct level," she said.
David expects the central bank to leave rates unchanged until after Brown's mini-budget, which she expects to deliver a fiscal tightening package of around 4.0 billion stg.
"If we don't get that, the pressure will be back on rates," she said.
The inflation report will be the first under the new regime and there is some confusion over whether it will be as explicit about the necessary policy prescription as it used to be.

Royal Bank of Scotland economist Marion Bell suggests it could contain a much more general analysis of the economy, more like the U.S. Federal Reserve chairman's Humphry Hawkins testimony, now that the Bank itself chooses interest rates.

"The nature of the report is going to have to change. The previous inflation report gave a forecast of inflation based on unchanged policy. If they continue that and forecast that we're going to miss the target then that is tantamount to telling the markets that they need to increase interest rates.
"It may be saying -- this is what we're worried about or looking at, rather than -- we're going to miss the inflaton target two years down the road," she said.

Bell argues that UK rates need to rise to around 6.75 percent by the end of the year because any fiscal tightening is unlikely to be able to knock burgeoning consumer demand on the head, particularly given the 10 billion stg due from windfall profits from merging building societies.
NatWest's Dicks argues rates only need to rise by another 1/4 point. "If the Bank is going to be consistent with the February report, it will say it hasn't done enough," Dicks said.
"Logic would make them pessimists tomorrow, but they may want to wait until the new monetary policy committee is constituted. They may just be biding their time," he said.
The new proposals put the conduct of monetary policy in the hands of a new, nine-member monetary policy committee which has yet to be formed.

As an interim measure, the Bank of England Governor, deputy Howard Davies and two executive directors -- Mervyn King and Ian Plenderleith -- will decide on policy. No date has yet been set for the June meeting.
The quarterly inflation report will be published at 1030 GMT on Tuesday.
